approaches.name: Lateral approach to the femur (thigh)
aliases: lateral approach to the femoral shaft
approaches.corridor: Extraperiosteal plane along the lateral femur, elevating vastus lateralis anteriorly off the lateral intermuscular septum

procedure_applications.condition: Lateral exposure of the proximal femur for extramedullary fixation
Open or minimally invasive lateral plating of the femoral shaft
Lateral exposure for plating around a femoral implant

positioning.text: Position the patient supine on a radiolucent table with a bump under the ipsilateral hip, or lateral, with the limb free-draped so length, rotation, and alignment can be controlled.

setup.text: Allow unobstructed fluoroscopy of the entire femur and drape the limb free for intraoperative manipulation and reduction.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the greater trochanter proximally and the lateral femoral condyle distally; the line connecting them defines the lateral femoral shaft and the incision axis.

incision.text: Make a longitudinal lateral incision along the line from the greater trochanter to the lateral femoral condyle, centered over the fracture or planned implant and extended only as far as needed.

superficial_interval.text: Incise the fascia lata and iliotibial tract in line with the skin incision to expose the vastus lateralis.

deep_interval.text: Reflect vastus lateralis anteriorly off the lateral intermuscular septum and elevate it extraperiosteally from the lateral femur; there is no true internervous plane because vastus lateralis is femoral-nerve innervated throughout.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata and iliotibial tract, vastus lateralis, and the periosteum of the lateral femur.

structures_encountered.text: Perforating branches of the profunda femoris cross from posterior to anterior through the lateral intermuscular septum and must be identified and controlled during vastus lateralis elevation.

structures_at_risk.text: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery are the principal structures at risk; avulsion causes brisk bleeding and retraction into the posterior compartment.
Femoral-nerve motor branches to vastus lateralis are endangered by dissection carried too far anteriorly or proximally into the muscle belly.

danger_zones.text: Control the profunda perforators as they traverse the lateral intermuscular septum before they are divided, because a retracted perforator bleeds into the posterior thigh and is difficult to retrieve.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid aggressive posterior retraction that tents the perforating vessels, and do not stray anteromedially toward the superficial femoral vessels in the adductor canal.

exposure.text: Provides access to the entire lateral femoral shaft for plate or nail fixation and is readily extensile both proximally and distally.

limitations.text: There is no true internervous plane, and the approach gives limited access to the posterior femur and the femoral vessels.

extensions.text: Extend proximally toward the greater trochanter and lateral proximal femur for intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric fixation, and distally toward the lateral condyle for distal-femoral exposure.

indications.text: Used for femoral-shaft plating (open or minimally invasive), intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric fixation, and periprosthetic femoral fracture fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Consider an alternative corridor when the lateral soft-tissue envelope is heavily contaminated or compromised, or when the target lies outside the lateral femur.

implant_implications.text: Supports lateral plate application and submuscular tunneling deep to vastus lateralis for minimally invasive osteosynthesis; preserve periosteal blood supply by limiting soft-tissue stripping.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm that positioning and draping allow unobstructed AP and lateral fluoroscopic views of the full femur before incision.

closure.text: Reapproximate vastus lateralis to the intermuscular septum where feasible, repair the fascia lata and iliotibial tract, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Approach-specific complications include perforator bleeding and thigh hematoma, quadriceps scarring with knee stiffness, iatrogenic vastus lateralis denervation, nonunion, and infection.

bailouts.text: If a perforating vessel bleeds and retracts, extend the exposure to identify and ligate it directly rather than blindly clamping toward the posterior compartment.

questions.question: Why is the lateral approach to the femur not a true internervous approach?
questions.answer: Because vastus lateralis is innervated by the femoral nerve throughout, so the plane is intramuscular/extraperiosteal rather than between two nerve territories.

questions.question: Which vessels are most at risk during the lateral approach to the femur?
questions.answer: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery as they cross the lateral intermuscular septum.
